video_title: Nvidia’s Next Problem: An Avalanche of Wafers
gist: Recorded right after Nvidia's earnings, Dan Nathan and Guy argue the blowout quarter (75% growth, ~75% gross margin, but a 300bp margin guide-down) is overshadowed by the CEO scandal, export-control/national-security probes, an SEC disclosure probe and an 'avalanche of wafers' inventory risk as customers second-source; they favor selling rallies, flag hyperscaler capex relief, weak cyber/software, and an Anthropic IPO likely to fade. The second half interviews Inkind's CEO Johan on its food-credit restaurant financing model, $750M+ Citi-led facility and $700M-$1B net revenue outlook.

themes.theme: Nvidia post-earnings: great print, governance and legal overhang

insights.claim: Nvidia's just-reported quarter showed ~75% year-over-year growth in sales and earnings with gross margins near 75%, but the company guided gross margins down ~300 basis points next quarter.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: A 300bp margin guide-down is the number to watch beneath a headline beat; margin compression may be the next leg of the story.
insights.quote: They did guide to margins down 300 basis points in the next quarter. That's a big guide.

insights.claim: Historically a quarter like this would lift Nvidia stock 15-20%, yet it was only up ~5% after hours near $162 after falling to ~$148, roughly a 40% haircut from its all-time high.
insights.speaker: Guy (co-host)
insights.so_what: Muted reaction to blowout numbers signals the market is pricing non-fundamental risk; fundamentals alone are not driving the stock.
insights.quote: Historically, this is a quarter that would get the stock up 15 to 20%.

insights.claim: Nvidia trades at roughly 10-11x next year's earnings, four to five turns below the market multiple, and had been going sideways for about nine months before the CEO scandal broke.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Cheap multiple reflects pre-existing doubts about the semi trade, not just the scandal; cheapness alone is not a catalyst.

insights.claim: Nvidia's CEO departure is tied to alleged affairs including one with an alleged Chinese spy connected to export-control circumvention (Singapore sales, remote GPU access by Chinese firms), creating national-security risk the hosts believe the market is not pricing.
insights.speaker: Guy (co-host)
insights.so_what: Expect congressional hearings, Commerce/FBI questions and headline 'tape bombs'; size Nvidia exposure for event risk.
insights.quote: In terms of the ramifications that potential national security risks bring with it, and I don't think the market is pricing that in as all.

insights.claim: Interim CEO and CFO Colette Crest likely had visibility into where chips and revenue (e.g., ~22% of sales, ~$10B, from Singapore in a 2025 quarter) were going, so her credibility is exposed as the SEC opens a probe into investor disclosures.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: An SEC disclosure probe implicates the CFO who signed the financials; leadership continuity at Nvidia is less stable than the interim appointment implies.
insights.quote: she clearly had to sign off on all the financials.

insights.claim: Nvidia's board averages ~14 years of tenure (double the S&P 500 average) and holds roughly $15B in stock and options, which Dan argues left it beholden to the former CEO and implies the issues are worse than disclosed.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Governance weakness raises odds of further revelations; board independence will be a focus of investigations.
insights.quote: So this board has been in his pocket.

insights.claim: The outcome hinges on 'who knew what and when' across Commerce (which allegedly backed off investigating Mega Speed at Nvidia's request), the FBI, Marco Rubio and the White House; if answered cleanly the stock is 'dirt cheap', if not it hurts the entire AI trade.
insights.speaker: Guy (co-host)
insights.so_what: Treat the investigation path as a binary for the whole AI complex, not just NVDA.
insights.quote: if they're answered appropriately, then the stock is dirt cheap.

insights.claim: Both hosts see a tradable ~10% bounce in Nvidia toward $175-180 but recommend selling rallies rather than calling this the capitulation 'clearing event' for semis.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Fade strength into $175-180; don't treat the print as an all-clear.
insights.quote: I think you sell rallies in it

insights.claim: Trump's shifting stance on whether he was briefed about the Nvidia matter, plus his meeting with President Xi in Shenzhen amid lobbying by Silicon Valley allies, adds regulatory/export-policy uncertainty for Nvidia.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Watch US-China summit headlines for export-policy shifts affecting Nvidia's China access.

themes.theme: 'Avalanche of wafers': second-sourcing and inventory risk for Nvidia

insights.claim: Nvidia's main customers are actively seeking second sources — AMD Radeon, Google TPUs, Amazon Trainium, and custom silicon from Broadcom and Marvell — which reportedly pushed the former CEO to seek new markets.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Customer diversification erodes Nvidia's share; custom-silicon suppliers are relative beneficiaries.

insights.claim: Nvidia reportedly has an 'avalanche of wafers' plus memory commitments; if demand undershoots guidance two to three quarters out, that becomes inventory bought when memory makers had pricing power, which will weigh on margins.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Track Nvidia inventory and purchase commitments vs. guidance; memory suppliers hold pricing power while Nvidia bears the inventory risk.
insights.quote: they have an avalanche of wafers

themes.theme: Hyperscalers and capex: who benefits if AI spend pulls back

insights.claim: Hyperscalers that went cash-flow negative funding AI buildouts could rally meaningfully if the Nvidia turmoil gives them a 'hall pass' to ratchet back capex.
insights.speaker: Guy (co-host)
insights.so_what: A capex pullback could be bullish for cash-burning hyperscalers even though it is bearish for chip suppliers.
insights.quote: they may now get a hall pass to say, you know what, maybe maybe we're going to ratchet back some of this

insights.claim: Google is ~30% off its May all-time high after funding its buildout with balance sheet, debt and equity; a capex cut would help cash flow but not the core worry that search faces existential AI risk.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Distinguish capex-relief rallies from fundamental search-share risk when owning GOOGL.

insights.claim: Meta rallied from ~$545 to ~$760 in a month on its Muse launch and has round-tripped to ~$620; with ~10M Muse accounts, Guy estimates usage must grow ~20x to matter for 3B+ MAU Meta.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Product-hype rallies in megacaps are fading; demand evidence of monetization before chasing.
insights.quote: That number has to be 20x what it is right now for to make an impact.

insights.claim: Meta's free personal assistant means more usage drives more token costs from AI capex without revenue, so scale increases losses unless it is monetized.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Free AI consumer products are a margin drag; watch for paid tiers or ad monetization of assistants.
insights.quote: the bigger it gets, meaning like the more folks that are using it, it's the more money they're going to lose on the thing.

insights.claim: Amazon is blocking third-party personal agents to defend its high-margin advertising business, while building its own small models and Trainium chips.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: AI agents threaten retail-media ad moats; platform gatekeeping is a defensive tell.
insights.quote: They've blocked out personal agents.

insights.claim: Oracle is the weak link among hyperscalers (down 3.5% on the day) and neoclouds would suffer most if the AI buildout falters.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Oracle and neoclouds are the highest-beta shorts/hedges against AI-capex disappointment.
insights.quote: if all this stuff doesn't work, Oracle's dead.

insights.claim: Despite a string of outages/possible hacks (FAA, Microsoft Outlook, United, NSA, Apple, Chase), cybersecurity stocks fell 30-40% in two months, led by Palo Alto, and the HACK ETF dropped from ~134 to ~113 with risk toward 100.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Security names are disconnected from threat headlines; valuation is the overhang.

insights.claim: Guy argues investors should re-engage with beaten-down cybersecurity names, citing John Chambers' emphasis on their importance, while Dan warns AI-adjacent stocks can still be cut in half as memory, storage and Intel showed.
insights.speaker: Guy (co-host)
insights.so_what: Contrarian long setup in security, but scale in given downside precedent.
insights.quote: I think you got to re-engage with those names.

insights.claim: Software ETF IGV has slipped back to ~$96-97 after its summer bounce, and Salesforce (CRM) fell ~9.5% in a day without news, apparently trading on generative-AI sentiment tied to its recent Anthropic partnership.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Software is trading as an AI-disruption casualty; partnerships with model labs aren't protecting multiples.
insights.quote: CRM was down nearly 10% today

themes.theme: Anthropic IPO as AI sentiment gauge

insights.claim: Anthropic was set to price its IPO with an indicated valuation around $1.4-1.5 trillion (versus a $2 trillion apex and a WSJ suggestion near $1 trillion), with ~$98 trading on Hyperliquid implying ~$2 trillion.
insights.speaker: Guy (co-host)
insights.so_what: Pricing and pre-market implied value are a real-time read on AI risk appetite.

insights.claim: Guy expects Anthropic to pop after pricing but fade back to the IPO price, mirroring SpaceX, which priced at $135, hit ~$225 in three days, then broke issue within a month; a weak pricing could re-accelerate the AI selloff.
insights.speaker: Guy (co-host)
insights.so_what: Don't chase the first-day pop; question who supports the stock beyond underwriters now that Nvidia is unlikely to backstop it.
insights.quote: I think it's going to be similarly short-lived and I think it settles back in to the IPO price.

themes.theme: Inkind: food-credit financing model for restaurants

insights.claim: Inkind finances restaurants by buying food-and-beverage credit at a discount (e.g., $1M advance for $2M of credit) with no repayment, equity, profit share or card swipes, then sells the credit to app users who get ~20% back.
insights.speaker: Johan (Inkind co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: A novel non-dilutive restaurant financing structure exploiting the gap between menu price and cost of goods.
insights.quote: we give a restaurant a million dollars, we buy $2 million in food.

insights.claim: The core economics: $2M of food at menu prices costs a restaurant only ~$600K to deliver, so the advance is cheap capital that also brings in customers.
insights.speaker: Johan (Inkind co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Explains why restaurants accept the deal and why unit economics can work at scale.
insights.quote: $2 million in food to a restaurant is worth $600,000.

insights.claim: Traditional restaurant investments fail because investors are paid from profits first on ~3-year payback/20% IRR terms, starving operators who then close; Johan's own 20 restaurant investments saw only 3 return capital.
insights.speaker: Johan (Inkind co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Avoid conventional restaurant equity deals; misaligned waterfalls drive closures.
insights.quote: the investors get paid out of the profits first and then the operator gets paid.

insights.claim: Inkind reports a 2.7% cumulative loss rate over 13 years, about 11,000 funded restaurants (1,926 signed in September alone), ~5.5M users, and a TAM of ~450,000 quality US restaurants.
insights.speaker: Johan (Inkind co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Large runway and low losses support its credit-facility expansion.

insights.claim: Inkind closed a ~$750M debt facility led by Citi, Cross River Bank and Liberty Mutual, is upsizing it to over $1B, holds a term sheet for another $750M, and just closed its first Series A after 13 years (Magnetar was its earlier lender and equity investor).
insights.speaker: Johan (Inkind co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Mainstream credit appetite for alternative fintech receivables; a potential future IPO candidate.
insights.quote: So suddenly it went from nobody wanted to give us capital to everybody wants.

insights.claim: Inkind projects $700M-$1B net revenue next year after a 132% CAGR, profitable for two years, and an unannounced bank card partnership could add up to 45M users.
insights.speaker: Johan (Inkind co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals the dining-rewards/credit-card benefit channel as a growth vector; watch for the partnership announcement.

insights.claim: Inkind's moat is that competitors would need years of deal-curve data to win bank financing plus a consumer base to sell credit into; unlike lenders, its risk falls as it scales because more users attract better restaurants.
insights.speaker: Johan (Inkind co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Network-effect plus data moat in a niche fintech; scale improves rather than worsens credit quality.
insights.quote: We're the opposite. Now, the bigger we get, the more consumers we have, the more profitable restaurants want to work with us

insights.claim: Johan's Austin restaurant Guest House does roughly 2x the revenue of a comparable competitor with more seats, which he attributes to Inkind-driven traffic, noting incremental revenue at a busy restaurant is highly profitable.
insights.speaker: Johan (Inkind co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Demand-drives-demand dynamics make customer acquisition, not just capital, the value proposition.

insights.claim: Johan prefers permanent-capital investors over VCs with 5-7 year fund lives, describing Inkind as being in 'the bottom of the first inning' after 13 years; he also notes Uber spent $20B building its consumer marketplace.
insights.speaker: Johan (Inkind co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Long-duration capital structures fit slow-compounding marketplaces; watch for founders avoiding VC timelines.
insights.quote: I don't want to be on someone else's timeline.
